newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran rug dealers await easing of forex restriction.
newsitem.headline: Iran rug dealers await easing of forex restriction.

text.p: Persian carpet exporters in Iran have adopted a wait-and-see attitude to a new law aimed at easing stiff currency rules that have stifled exports, Tehran's second cash earner after oil, dealers said on Thursday.
The dealers said they were waiting to see if the law would actually take effect despite a wrangle between the government and parliament, which passed the law this week.

A high government council must still ratify the law, which does away with currency restrictions blamed for rug exports tumbling to $968 million in the last Iranian year which ended on March 19, 1996 from $1.6 billion in the previous year.
"There have been so many changes of rules and regulations by authorities that it is hard for carpet dealers to trust any new promises," a rug exporter said.
"Of course it would be a welcome move but we still have to see if the Guardian Council approves it even though the government is opposed to it," the exporter told Reuters.

Central Bank Governor Mohsen Nourbakhsh has predicted that the council, a body of clerics and lawyers which vets parliament decisions for conformity with Islam and the Constitution, would reject the law.

The law aims to ease the crisis in Iran's carpet industry by elimininating rules which force exporters to return all but 30 percent of their hard cash income to Iran and exchange it at an unfavourable official rate in state banks.

But Nourbakhsh said the law, which allows exporters to keep their hard cash income and use it to import raw materials for carpet production and other required goods, would weaken the Iranian currency and cause other economic problems.
The regulations were imposed in 1995 to stop a flight of hard currency after the Iranian rial plummetted in the wake of the announcement of United States sanctions against Iran.
The government has in the past few months partially yielded to pressures from carpet dealers and announced it was easing some aspects of the regulations.

But official figures published by newspapers this week showed that exports of carpets and other handicrafts had continued to fall, reaching only $476 million in the first nine months of the current year which began on March 20, 1996.
Traders and exporters have expressed concern over the fall of the exports and urged for measures to support the carpet weaving industry which employs about two million people.
